title: Ezra 2:59–70
context: The list closes with families who cannot prove their descent, priests set aside from the most holy things until a priest serves with Urim and Thummim, and the totals of the assembly, the servants, the animals, and the gifts for the work. Some who came up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer “could not show their fathers’ houses and their offspring, whether they were of Israel.” Priestly houses in the same position are named, including a line that took the name of Barzillai the Gileadite by marriage. The whole assembly is “forty-two thousand three hundred sixty,” the same total as Nehemiah 7:66, yet the named groups earlier in this chapter, taken as they stand, do not add up to that figure, and many of the line-item counts differ from Nehemiah 7 even where the grand total agrees. The gap should be named and left unresolved, not filled by a theory the text does not give. The servant and animal figures, and then the free gifts of gold, silver, and garments, stand beside a differently structured offering notice in Nehemiah 7:70–72. The people settle in their cities. Both traditions read the close of the list as a historical enrollment and a shared confession that the LORD has brought a people home, without a contrast over the names or the counts.

verses.text: These were those who went up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer; but they could not show their fathers’ houses and their offspring, whether they were of Israel:
verses.arminianNotes:
Some went up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, “but they could not show their fathers’ houses and their offspring, whether they were of Israel”. Nehemiah 7:61 has the same five places, with Addon rather than Addan, and the same problem of proof. The list is careful to mark those whose Israelite descent could not be shown.

Arminian readers take the admission as a real limit in the record, not as a slight to be smoothed away, and they keep WEB’s Addan here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set Addan and Addon side by side and hear the same caution: these families could not show their fathers’ houses or their offspring.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the place-name, and they do not invent a genealogy the verse says was lacking.

verses.text: the children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred fifty-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
The families are the children of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, six hundred fifty-two. Nehemiah 7:62 names the same three houses at six hundred forty-two. A Nekoda has already appeared among the temple servants in 2:48; the two lines are not assumed to be one. The two totals should be left unharmonized.

Arminian readers take six hundred fifty-two as this book’s count of the unproven houses, and they refuse to correct it from Nehemiah 7.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name both figures and keep the three family names as a historical group whose descent could not be shown.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the ten-person difference and do not merge this Nekoda with the earlier servant house.

verses.text: Of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Hakkoz, and the children of Barzillai, who took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name.
verses.arminianNotes:
Among the priests are the children of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, “who took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name.” Nehemiah 7:63 has the same story, with Hobaiah rather than Habaiah. The name Barzillai the Gileadite recalls the man who helped David in 2 Samuel 17 and 19; this verse explains the priestly house’s name by that marriage, without filling in later generations.

Arminian readers keep Habaiah as WEB gives it, and they take the marriage notice as the reason this house bears Barzillai’s name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Habaiah and Hobaiah unharmonized and read the Barzillai link as the verse states it, a name taken from the daughters of that Gileadite house.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spelling and do not build a full family tree beyond the line.

verses.text: These sought their place among those who were registered by genealogy, but they were not found; therefore they were deemed disqualified and removed from the priesthood.
verses.arminianNotes:
“These sought their place among those who were registered by genealogy, but they were not found; therefore they were deemed disqualified and removed from the priesthood.” The search itself is reported, and the result is exclusion from priestly service. Nehemiah 7:64 says the same in slightly different words. The decision is not softened, and another outcome is not invented.

Arminian readers take the disqualification as a real judgment based on a missing record, a serious limit on those who could not be found in the register.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a careful guard on the priesthood: those not found in the genealogy are removed, the same outcome as in Nehemiah 7:64.

Both traditions keep the verse as a historical exclusion, not as a type of later church discipline to be pressed here.

verses.text: The governor told them that they should not eat of the most holy things until a priest stood up to serve with Urim and with Thummim.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The governor told them that they should not eat of the most holy things until a priest stood up to serve with Urim and with Thummim.” The governor is not named here, and he is not identified as Sheshbazzar, Zerubbabel, or some later official as if the verse had done so. Urim and Thummim are the priestly means of decision already known from the law; the excluded priests must wait until a priest serves with them. Nehemiah 7:65 is a close parallel.

Arminian readers take the ban as a real, temporary limit on the most holy things, pending a priestly decision the governor himself does not claim to give.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the governor unnamed and hear the same restraint: the most holy things are withheld until Urim and Thummim are in use, a limit the law itself supplies.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the office or the waiting, and they do not fill in a name the text withholds.

verses.text: The whole assembly together was forty-two thousand three hundred sixty,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The whole assembly together was forty-two thousand three hundred sixty,” the same grand total as Nehemiah 7:66. The named groups earlier in this chapter, counted as they stand, come to a good deal less than that figure, and many of those line-items also differ from Nehemiah 7. The agreement in the total and the disagreement in the parts should both be reported. Readers have offered various accounts of the gap; this verse does not explain it, and no solution is chosen here.

Arminian readers take forty-two thousand three hundred sixty as the total this book actually states, and they refuse to hide that the preceding figures do not add up to it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the shared total beside the unsummed lists and leave the difference unresolved, consistent with the way the earlier notes have treated Nehemiah 7.

Both traditions invent no theological contrast over the counts and do not force a harmony the text does not give.

verses.text: in addition to their male servants and their female servants, of whom there were seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven; and they had two hundred singing men and singing women.
verses.arminianNotes:
In addition there were seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven male and female servants, and “two hundred singing men and singing women.” The servant total matches Nehemiah 7:67; that verse has two hundred forty-five singing men and singing women. The singers here are named in addition to the assembly of 2:64, and the two singer figures should be left unharmonized.

Arminian readers take the seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven as a real additional company, and they keep this verse’s two hundred singers rather than the larger Nehemiah number.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreed servant count and the different singer total, and they refuse to treat either difference or agreement as a doctrinal issue.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the figures and do not fold the servants into the forty-two thousand three hundred sixty as if the verse had done so.

verses.text: Their horses were seven hundred thirty-six; their mules, two hundred forty-five;
verses.arminianNotes:
Their horses were seven hundred thirty-six, and their mules two hundred forty-five, the same figures as Nehemiah 7:68. The animal counts are part of the same closing inventory, not a symbol of strength or of weakness.

Arminian readers take the horses and mules as a real count of what the returnees had with them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:68 and keep the line in the register of the list, a record of animals, not a type.

Both traditions invent no contrast over matching figures and do not press the numbers into a lesson.

verses.text: their camels, four hundred thirty-five; their donkeys, six thousand seven hundred twenty.
verses.arminianNotes:
Their camels were four hundred thirty-five, and their donkeys six thousand seven hundred twenty, again the same figures as Nehemiah 7:69. The two books meet in the whole animal inventory, even after many human counts have differed.

Arminian readers take the camels and donkeys as a further historical total, the last of the animal figures in this chapter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the agreed counts and leave them as inventory, beside the earlier differences in the people-lists.

Both traditions invent no contrast over numbers that match, and they do not allegorize the animals.

verses.text: Some of the heads of fathers’ households, when they came to the LORD’s house which is in Jerusalem, offered willingly for God’s house to set it up in its place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Some of the heads of fathers’ households, when they came “to the LORD’s house which is in Jerusalem, offered willingly for God’s house to set it up in its place.” The site is already in view, even before the work of chapter 3, and the gifts are willing, in the same register as the free will offering of 1:4–6. Nehemiah 7:70–72 will describe related gifts in a different arrangement.

Arminian readers hear a real, willing offering from some of the heads, aimed at setting the house up in its place, not a levy forced on every family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stress the purpose: the gifts are for God’s house, in Jerusalem, to set it up in its place, the first movement toward the rebuilding that follows.

Both traditions take the verse as shared ground in generous devotion, without a contrast over who gave.

verses.text: They gave according to their ability into the treasury of the work sixty-one thousand darics of gold, five thousand minas of silver, and one hundred priests’ garments.
verses.arminianNotes:
They gave “according to their ability into the treasury of the work sixty-one thousand darics of gold, five thousand minas of silver, and one hundred priests’ garments.” Darics are Persian gold coins; a mina is a large silver weight. No modern total is pressed as if the verse had given one. Nehemiah 7:70–72 splits gifts among the governor, some heads, and the rest of the people, with different amounts of gold and silver and a different count of garments. The two notices should be named and not forced into one sum.

Arminian readers take this verse’s three figures as the offering Ezra records, given according to ability, and they refuse to rewrite them from Nehemiah 7.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the sixty-one thousand darics, five thousand minas, and one hundred garments unharmonized with the split totals in Nehemiah 7:70–72.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the amounts and keep the gifts as a historical contribution to the work.

verses.text: So the priests and the Levites, with some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants, lived in their cities, and all Israel in their cities.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the priests and the Levites, with some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants, lived in their cities, and all Israel in their cities.” The return ends in settlement, each group in its cities, and “all Israel” is named with them. Nehemiah 7:73 is a close parallel, with a further notice that when the seventh month had come, the children of Israel were in their cities, a line this verse does not add and that Ezra 3:1 will take up in its own way.

Arminian readers take the settlement as a real close of the journey, priests, Levites, and people at home in their cities.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear all Israel named at the end of the list, a people back in their cities, and they leave the seventh-month notice to Nehemiah 7:73 and to the next chapter.

Both traditions close the unit as shared ground: the LORD has brought a people home, and the differences of count along the way have not been turned into a party argument.
